passage:
For forty-one years, Ida Brannock walked out to the white box on the schoolhouse lawn in Wendle Cross at nine each morning, read the two instruments inside, a rain gauge and a thermometer, and wrote both figures in a handwritten ledger begun in 1938. In all that time the record shows one gap: eleven blank lines one February, when a fall on the ice kept her in hospital. Her rule was that no other person's figures went into the ledger, so the lines stayed empty.

This spring, at seventy-eight, she stepped down as keeper, and the district weather office at Lowmarch wrote a letter to the parish council. Pointing to the eleven blank lines, it doubted whether a record kept by one person's hand could go on without some check, and said it would decide next March whether to keep Wendle Cross in its tables. Ida's wish, she told the council, was simply that it should.

The idea of a sensor came from Neve Callan, who teaches the older class at the village school. She would walk out at nine herself for a year while a sensor stood beside the box on trial, so that each of her readings could be checked against the machine's. The council voted for her plan, its chair explaining that the office would drop any figures it could not check.

Her pupils graph the two columns every Friday. Since the autumn the lines have drifted apart, and the office has written to the council with the charge that Neve's figures run a degree high, because the old box stands nearer the school's boiler vent than the sensor does.

The trial ends in March. Each morning Neve writes her figure in the handwritten ledger with the sensor's beside it, and the difference between them has reached a degree and a half. The ledger has ruled pages enough for another four years of mornings.

passage:
For many summers Tamsin Rowe has led a July walk through the Hatherby cutting, where a railway once ran between an old platform and a brick footbridge. Volunteers with red torches walk it in about 28 minutes, marking each green light on a map. Rowe's first walk found 23, and the usual total is now about ninety. Last July the count fell to 35.

The Hatherby Line Trust acted within days. Its first step was to pay for 16 snail boards, and its committee asked Rowe to lay them along the banks that week.

Every light is a wingless female glow-worm. What she needs is a tall grass stem to climb after full dark, where she glows to draw flying males; her larvae live in the turf and feed on snails. It had been a dry spring, and the cutting had changed. In March the Hatherby Line Trust put up 42 solar lamps at the platform end; in April it widened the path with gravel; in May its contractor did the mowing of the banks, usually left until September. Because the trust now locks the platform gate at ten, the walk had also moved an hour earlier, to half past nine.

Even after the dry spring, the boards came up crowded. On the maps, the losses were spread evenly: under the lamps and past them, on the mown banks and on the steep strip below the footbridge beyond reach of the mowing, along the new gravel and on the far bank well away from it. At half past nine in July the sky is still pale. So the gate was left open one night, and a volunteer held the footbridge rail and watched the banks below light up one by one; the walk at the old hour of half past ten counted close to the usual ninety.

The trust will open the gate for the walk each July; on every other night it stays locked at ten. For years villagers walked the cutting after dark, children on their parents' shoulders counting lights to the footbridge, and Rowe's oldest maps carry their pencilled tallies, in hands she can still name.

passage:
The radio warned of frost at supper: minus four by dawn, with the apricots in full blossom. Tomas went to the window first and looked across the lane at Mrs. Odell's orchard. Then he read the thermometer nailed to the gate and walked down to the young trees in the far row. In the barn he counted the cans of oil: eleven, enough for the burners under half the orchard. He came back last to look over the blossoms on the corner tree his father had planted by the gate.

The old tree had given little fruit for years, and the best of it went to the birds. It would not come through this one, Tomas thought, whatever we did. Still, his plan put two-thirds of the burners in a ring round it, each set with care, and the rest reached only down the far row, where the cold settled first. Tomas and I drew straws for the first watch.

Mrs. Odell came across the lane at eleven. Her own orchard was lit with her own oil. She had come to share the watch and help, but Tomas sat her beside him instead. She remembered his father planting the corner tree the spring the lane was graveled, carrying it up from the station in a bucket.

Toward dawn the frost came down harder than the radio had warned, and the thermometer on the gate read minus five. Both of them had judged that the old tree would be lost, and neither left it. Tomas spent the last hours guarding it, refilling each burner as it needed oil.

By morning the far row had come through, saved by the few burners we could spare it. The blossoms on the corner tree were brown by noon. The next frost held off until the fruit had set, and the burners stayed in the barn until they were lit again the next spring. Tomas cut the old tree down that winter. I still keep a twig of it pressed in a book, taken at midnight, when it stood white in the ring of flame and Mrs. Odell was telling us about the bucket.
